A former Kopassus special-forces officer, he became Indonesia's oldest first-term president when he took office in 2024 — which leader?
Prabowo Subianto: President of Indonesia since 2024. In early 2008, Prabowo's inner circle established the Gerindra Party.
Imprisoned by British authorities during both the Salt Satyagraha and the Quit India movement, this independence leader became India's first president in 1950 — who is he?
Rajendra Prasad: President of India from 1950 to 1962.
He oversaw the Apollo 11 Moon landing and the birth of the EPA, yet he's the only person ever to step down from the U.S. presidency — which president?
Richard Nixon: President of the United States from 1969 to 1974.
After Germany's defeat, this SS officer lived under a false name until the British found him and handed him to Polish authorities, who tried and executed him — who was he?
Rudolf Höss: Nazi commandant of Auschwitz (1901–1947)
Named for a 1930s guerrilla leader who resisted US occupation, this Nicaraguan socialist party toppled the Somoza dynasty in 1979 and governed through the 1980s — which party?
Sandinista National Liberation Front: Nicaraguan socialist political party founded in 1961.
This Russian nihilist preached revolution "by any means necessary" and fled the country in 1869 after taking part in the murder of a former comrade who'd dared to disagree with him — who was he?

Sparked in 1991 when the Revolutionary United Front — backed by Liberia's Charles Taylor — moved to topple the Momoh government, this nearly 11-year conflict displaced some 2.5 million people. Which war is it?
Sierra Leone Civil War: 1991–2002 war in West Africa.

He out-debated and beat Abraham Lincoln for an 1858 Senate seat, then lost to him for the presidency two years later — and helped broker the Compromise of 1850 along the way. Which Illinois Democrat was he?
Stephen A. Douglas: American politician and lawyer (1813–1861)
A teacher, Marxist, and philosopher honored as a "Father of the Republic of Indonesia," this independence fighter founded the Murba Party and lived the life of a guerrilla and spy — who was he?
Tan Malaka: Indonesian communist philosopher, activist, and national hero (1897–1949)
Rising from Henry VIII's almoner to Lord Chancellor, this English cardinal controlled nearly every matter of state and held the Archbishopric of York — until his fall from royal favor. Who was he?
Thomas Wolsey: English statesman and cardinal (1473–1530)
This Indian revolutionary assassinated the former Punjab lieutenant governor in 1940 in revenge for the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre, of which he was a survivor — who was he?
Udham Singh: Indian revolutionary (1899–1940). Singh was subsequently tried and convicted of murder and hanged in July 1940.

Dubbed the 'Merchant of Death' after a 2003 UN report, this former Soviet military translator smuggled weapons from Eastern Europe to Africa and the Middle East before a 2008 Thailand sting — who is he?
One of the most popular presidents at his death in 1923, this Ohio newspaperman who built up the Marion Star saw his reputation later wrecked by exposed scandals — who was he?
Warren G. Harding: President of the United States from 1921 to 1923.
The longest-serving member of any democratic German parliament, this CDU politician served as president of the Bundestag from 2017 to 2021 — who was he?
Dismembered by the Titans and reborn, this figure from Greek myth was sometimes identified with an Orphic version of Dionysus and linked by Aeschylus to Hades — who is he?
Zagreus: Figure in Greek mythology. In the earliest mention of Zagreus, he is paired with Gaia and called the "highest" god, though perhaps only in reference to the gods of the underworld.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Henrietta Swan Leavitt (born 1868) is the earliest of the four. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (July 4, 1868 – December 12, 1921) was an American astronomer.
Which of these people was born first?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four began earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four. It is named after French mathematician, philosopher and physicist Blaise Pascal.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Galileo Galilei is an astronomer. Galileo has been called the father of observational astronomy, modern-era classical physics, the scientific method, and modern science.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Blaise Pascal is a mathematician. Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 – 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
What is the atomic number of Unbinilium?
Unbinilium, also known as eka-radium or element 120, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubn and atomic number 120.
What is the atomic number of Arsenic?
Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.
In what year was Ted Kaczynski born?
Ted Kaczynski: The FBI used the case identifier UNABOM (University and Airline Bombing) before his identity was known, resulting in the media naming him the "Unabomber".
In what year was Steve Wozniak born?
Steve Wozniak: In 1976, he co-founded Apple Computer (now Apple Inc.) with his early business partner Steve Jobs.
In what year was Dmitri Mendeleev born?
Dmitri Mendeleev: The synthetic element mendelevium is named in his honor.
In what year did Ptolemy die?
Ptolemy: The first was his astronomical treatise now known as the Almagest, originally entitled Mathēmatikḗ Syntaxis (Μαθηματικὴ Σύνταξις, 'Mathematical Treatise').
In what year did Al-Khwarizmi die?
Al-Khwarizmi: Few biographical details are known about al-Khwarizmi's life.
In what year was Nitrogen discovered?
Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Which company manufactures Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk?
Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk: Skunk Works. It was the first operational aircraft to be designed with stealth technology.
In which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21 based?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21: Soviet Union. Approximately 60 countries across four continents have flown the MiG-21, and it still serves many nations seven decades after its maiden flight.
Who is credited with discovering Triangulum Australe?
Triangulum Australe: Américo Vespucio. Triangulum Australe is a small constellation in the far Southern Celestial Hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Ichthyosaurus?
Ichthyosaurus: Mary Anning. It is among the best known ichthyosaur genera, as it is the type genus of the order Ichthyosauria.
Who is credited with discovering Theobroma cacao?
Theobroma cacao: Christopher Columbus. Theobroma cacao (cacao tree or cocoa tree) is a small (6–12 m (20–39 ft) tall) evergreen tree in the Malvaceae family.
Who is credited with discovering Krypton?
Krypton: William Ramsay. Krypton (from Ancient Greek: κρυπτός, romanized: kryptos 'the hidden one') is a chemical element; it has symbol Kr and atomic number 36.

A German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the theory of relativity, his mass–energy formula E=mc2 comes from special relativity and has been called "the world's most famous equation." Born in 1879, who won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics?
Albert Einstein (14 March 1879 - 18 April 1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the known theory of relativity.
Whether from too few red blood cells or faulty hemoglobin, this disorder leaves the blood less able to carry oxygen — often felt as quiet tiredness long before any paleness shows — what is it?
Anemia (also spelt anaemia in British English) is a blood disorder in which the blood has a reduced ability to carry oxygen.

A German former computer repair technician, this man received international attention after murdering and cannibalizing a voluntary victim he had found over the Internet in March 2001, and was ultimately convicted of murder in a 2006 retrial — who is he?

Armin Meiwes (born 1 December 1961) is a German former computer repair technician who received international attention for murdering and cannibalising Bernd Brandes, whom he had found via the Internet as a voluntary victim, in March 2001.
Only eight species of this stocky-legged, shaggy, short-tailed carnivoran survive, ranging across North and South America and Eurasia — what mammal is it?
Bear are carnivoran mammals of the family Ursidae.
This insect order contains both cockroaches and termites — the latter now classified as a specialized, social lineage within the former group — what order is it?
Blattodea is an order of insects that contains cockroaches and termites.
Affecting roughly 22% of people worldwide and often striking during sleep, this parafunctional habit grinds teeth and clenches jaws until enamel wears away — what's it called?
Bruxism is excessive teeth grinding or jaw clenching.

This American astronomer and planetary scientist was initially an assistant professor at Harvard before moving to Cornell as the David Duncan Professor of Astronomy. He played an active role in the Voyager programs. Who is he?
Carl Sagan (November 9, 1934 - December 20, 1996) was an American astronomer, planetary scientist and science communicator.

Once prized as refrigerants and aerosol propellants — Freon being the famous example — these halogenated compounds were phased out under the Montreal Protocol for gnawing holes in the ozone layer — what are they?
Chlorofluorocarbon (CFCs) and hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) are fully or partly halogenated hydrocarbons that contain carbon (C), hydrogen (H), chlorine (Cl), and fluorine (F).
In mathematics, this term describes a selection of items from a set in which the order of choosing doesn't matter — unlike its counterpart, the permutation. Name the concept?
Combination is a selection of items from a set that has distinct members, such that the order of selection does not matter (unlike permutations).

This practice and field of study focuses on techniques for secure communication in the presence of adversaries, sitting at the intersection of mathematics, computer science, and electrical engineering — what's the field called?
Cryptography is the practice and study of techniques for secure communication in the presence of adversarial behavior.
A colorless liquid that's a workhorse solvent for chemical reactions, this compound is officially odorless — yet degraded samples reek of fish thanks to a dimethylamine impurity; what is it?
Dimethylformamide is an organic compound with the chemical formula HCON(CH3)2.
Despite common belief, this shocking South American fish belongs to the knifefish order and is more closely related to catfish than its name implies — what is it?
Electric eel are a genus, Electrophorus, of neotropical freshwater fish from South America in the family Gymnotidae, of which they are the only members of the subfamily Electrophorinae.
This sweet-tasting but toxic diol is a workhorse of antifreeze and polyester manufacturing, and astronomers have even detected the molecule in space — what is it?
Ethylene glycol (IUPAC name: ethane-1,2-diol) is an organic compound (a vicinal diol) with the formula (CH2OH)2.
Encompassing everything from oral tales and proverbs to festival rituals and traditional building styles, what term describes the shared expressive culture of a group?
Folklore is the body of expressive culture shared by a particular group of people, culture or subculture.
Ordained a priest in 1923, this Belgian physicist connected an expanding universe to Einstein's field equations and floated an early Big Bang hypothesis — who was he?
Georges Lemaître (lə-MET-rə; 17 July 1894 - 20 June 1966) was a Belgian Catholic priest, theoretical physicist, and mathematician who made major contributions to cosmology and astrophysics.

This German physicist turned his eye on the mind itself, founding psychophysics and giving his name to a law showing that sensation rises with the logarithm — not the raw intensity — of a stimulus. Whose pioneering work was it?
Gustav Fechner (19 April 1801 - 18 November 1887) was a German physicist, philosopher, and experimental psychologist.
Sometimes called urticaria, this itchy rash of raised welts can flare for minutes or days, may follow an allergy or infection, and in half of all cases has no identifiable cause — what is it?
Hives is a kind of skin rash with red or flesh-colored, raised, itchy bumps.

For decades this University of Virginia psychiatrist ran a Division of Perceptual Studies and gathered evidence that memories — and even bodily features — might carry across lives. Which researcher into reincarnation was he?

Ian Stevenson (October 31, 1918 - February 8, 2007) was a Canadian-born American psychiatrist, the founder and director of the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia School of Medicine.
This Canadian-American physical educator invented an entire sport, wrote its original rule book after moving to the United States, and founded the University of Kansas's program in 1898 — who is he?
James Naismith (November 6, 1861 - November 28, 1939) was a Canadian-American physical educator, physician, Christian chaplain, and sports coach, best known as the inventor of the game of basketball.
One species of this succulent plant genus, native mainly to Madagascar, became one of the first plants ever sent into space aboard a Soviet space station in 1979 — what genus is it?
Kalanchoe (also called "kalanche" or "kalancho"), is a genus of about 125 species of tropical, succulent plants in the stonecrop family Crassulaceae, mainly native to Madagascar and tropical Africa.
Closely related to earthworms but equipped with a sucker at each end, these segmented parasitic or predatory worms make up their own subclass within the annelid phylum — what are they?
Leech are segmented parasitic or predatory worms that comprise the subclass Hirudinea within the phylum Annelida.
Based on a commercial airliner design, this four-engine turboprop aircraft hunts submarines for the U.S. Navy using a distinctive tail-mounted magnetic detector — what plane is it?
Lockheed P-3 Orion is a four-engined, turboprop anti-submarine and maritime surveillance aircraft developed for the United States Navy and introduced in the 1960s.

With over 2,400 species sporting triangular heads, bulging eyes on flexible necks, and folded forelegs built to snatch prey, these insects count termites and cockroaches among their closest relatives — what are they?
Mantis are an order (Mantodea) of insects that contains over 2,400 species in about 460 genera in 33 families.
Sold dissolved in solution or shipped anhydrous in pressurized railcars, this simplest primary amine reeks like rotten fish — what compound is it?
Methylamine is an organic compound with a formula of CH5N or CH3NH2.
Containing antimicrobial lysozymes and immunoglobulins, most of this protective body fluid is produced in the gastrointestinal tract — what is it called?
Mucus is a slippery fluid produced by, and covering, mucous membranes.
Also called niacin, this organic compound is an essential vitamin B3 that plants and animals produce from the amino acid tryptophan. What is it?
Nicotinic acid is an organic compound and a vitamer of vitamin B3, an essential human nutrient.
This flowering herb in the mint family, native to the Mediterranean, is sometimes called wild marjoram and is a staple of countless savory dishes. What is it?
Oregano (Origanum vulgare) is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae.
Which American biologist became famous for the controversial 1968 book 'The Population Bomb' and its dire warnings about population growth, famine, and resource depletion?

Paul R. Ehrlich (May 29, 1932 - March 13, 2026) was an American biologist, author, and environmentalist known for his predictions and warnings about the consequences of population growth, including famine and resource depletion.

Derived from phosphoric acid by removing one to three protons, this anion or salt takes forms like dihydrogen and hydrogen variants and gives its name to fertilizers and various esters — name the ion?
Phosphate is an anion, salt, functional group or ester derived from a phosphoric acid.
This spiny rodent actually comes in two unrelated varieties, an Old World family and a New World family, whose lookalike coats of keratin quills evolved independently — what animal is it?
Porcupine are large rodents with coats of sharp spines, or quills, that protect them against predators.
This opening at the center of the iris lets light reach the retina and appears black — round in people, a slit in cats, and even a ring shape in some catfish — what's it called?
Pupil is a hole located in the center of the iris of the eye that allows light to strike the retina.
Also called king's crown or Arctic root, this Arctic-growing perennial is widely sold as a supplement even though regulators say its health claims lack solid evidence — which plant?
Rhodiola rosea (commonly golden root, rose root, roseroot, Aaron's rod, Arctic root, king's crown, lignum rhodium, orpin rose) is a perennial flowering plant in the family Crassulaceae.
Having taught economics at the Catholic University of Asunción and once served as Paraguay's finance minister, this politician assumed his country's presidency in 2023 — who is he?
Santiago Peña (Spanish; born 16 November 1978) is a Paraguayan politician and economist who has served as the 52nd president of Paraguay since 2023.
This macrofungus, native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, is now cultivated and consumed around the globe as one of its most widely eaten mushrooms. What mushroom is this?
Shiitake is a macrofungus native to East Asia and mainland Southeast Asia, which is cultivated and consumed around the globe.

This now-discredited scientific theory held that living creatures like fleas or maggots could regularly arise directly from non-living matter such as dust or rotting flesh, and was coherently synthesized by Aristotle. Name the theory?
Spontaneous generation is a superseded scientific theory that held that living creatures could arise from non-living matter and that such processes were commonplace and regular.

This amniote lineage — one of just two major branches alongside the reptile-and-bird clade — is marked by a single temporal opening behind the eye and gave rise to every mammal alive today — name the group?
Synapsida is a diverse group of tetrapod vertebrates that includes all mammals and their extinct relatives.
Writing in 1798, this English cleric-economist warned that abundance only fuels population growth, eventually restoring poverty and hardship for the lower classes — who is he?
Thomas Robert Malthus (13/14 February 1766 - 29 December 1834) was an English economist, cleric, and scholar influential in the fields of political economy and demography.
Egypt and Iraq both flew this Soviet-designed jet bomber in wars against Israel, and China still produces an updated license-built version, the H-6K — which aircraft?
Tupolev Tu-16 (USAF/DOD reporting name Type 39; NATO reporting name: Badger) is a twin-engined jet strategic heavy bomber used by the Soviet Union.
This canid genus contains the 'true foxes' — smaller and bushier-tailed than any wolf or jackal, typically living two to four years, occasionally a decade — which genus?
Vulpes is a genus of the subfamily Caninae.

This Polish-American scholar served as Jimmy Carter's national security advisor from 1977 to 1981 and helped organize an influential international policy group known as the Trilateral Commission — who is he?
Zbigniew Brzezinski (March 28, 1928 - May 26, 2017) was a Polish-American diplomat and political scientist.
This term for cancer that begins in gland cells applies to the most common form of breast cancer and one of the two major types of esophageal cancer — which term?
De Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter
Adenocarcinoma: Cancer of epithelial cells with glandular origin or characteristics.

Often called the greatest mathematician of the twentieth century, this German-born Frenchman revolutionized algebraic geometry before abruptly leaving his post at a Paris research institute in 1970 — who is he?

These coiled-shelled cephalopods, more closely related to octopuses than to nautiluses despite the resemblance, thrived from the Devonian until vanishing around the dinosaur extinction 66 million years ago — what are they?
Ammonoidea: Extinct subclass of cephalopod molluscs.
Known by the symbol Sb and mined chiefly from stibnite ore, which element has long been powdered into the cosmetic kohl and today hardens lead in car batteries?
Antimony: Chemical element with atomic number 51 (Sb)
These chitin-armored invertebrates must shed their exoskeletons to grow and circulate haemolymph through an open body cavity — and may number up to ten million species. What are they?
Arthropod: Phylum of invertebrates with jointed exoskeletons.

Flown by the Royal Air Force's Red Arrows display team, this British jet-powered advanced trainer has been license-built in India by Hindustan Aeronautics, with over 1,000 sold to 18 countries — which aircraft?
BAE Systems Hawk: Military training aircraft family.

This Swiss-American engineer was the only one of a famous physicist's three known biological grandsons to survive childhood, and later earned patents in electronics while working at Texas Instruments — who was he?

Developed to supplement the 727 on short routes, this narrow-body twinjet kept the 707's fuselage width and six-abreast seating and entered service with Lufthansa in 1968 — which best-selling aircraft is it?
A tree-like cluster of dark-green flower heads sprouting from a thick pale stalk, this cabbage-family vegetable is a close cousin of cauliflower and can be eaten raw or cooked — what is it?
Broccoli: Edible green plant in the cabbage family.
Named to honor the Virgin Mary and her golden crown, this daisy-family flower is also known as the pot marigold — which plant?
Calendula officinalis: Species of flowering plant in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Known also as yoke elm, this species of hornbeam native to Western Asia and Europe grows only up to elevations of about 1,000 metres — which species?
Carpinus betulus: Species of tree. It requires a warm climate for good growth, and occurs only at elevations up to 1,000 metres (3,300 ft).
Often called 'the father of the computer,' this English polymath designed the difference engine and the analytical engine, borrowing a punch-card principle from the Jacquard loom — who is he?
Charles Babbage: English mathematician, philosopher, and engineer (1791–1871)
One of the original citrus fruits, this large fragrant relative of the lemon has a thick, coarse rind and is a genetic ancestor of most modern citrus hybrids — what is it?
In mathematics, this is a selection of items from a set where the order of choosing them does not matter, unlike a permutation — what is it called?

Combination: Selection of items from a set. In mathematics, a combination is a selection of items from a set that has distinct members, such that the order of selection does not matter (unlike permutations).
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on where you stand, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Americas — what is it?
Cougar: Wild cat species native to the Americas.
Native to Mexico and Central America, this tuberous flowering plant blooms in nearly every hue except blue, and its tubers store energy as inulin rather than starch — what is it?
Dahlia: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.

Historically defined by having two embryonic seed leaves, this once-standard division of flowering plants covers around 200,000 species but turned out not to share one common ancestor — which plant group?
Dicotyledon: Historical grouping of flowering plants.
One of the very first vertebrate apex predators on Earth, this armor-plated, jointed-neck fish patrolled open Devonian seas some 380 million years ago — which genus?
This Russian economist served as Vladimir Putin's economic adviser before becoming governor of the Central Bank of Russia — who is she?

Elvira Nabiullina: Russian economist and Governor of the Bank of Russia. Elvira Sakhipzadovna Nabiullina (born 29 October 1963) is a Russian economist and current governor of the Central Bank of Russia.
This branch of anthropology studies individual cultures through participant observation, with roots in early 20th-century social science — what is this field called?
Ethnography: Systematic study of people and cultures.
Birds of prey in the genus Falco, some small species are called hobbies and hover-hunters are called kestrels — what are they collectively known as?
Falcon: Birds of prey in the genus Falco. The largest falcon is the gyrfalcon at up to 65 cm (26 in) in length.
Members of the order Siphonaptera, these flightless blood-sucking parasites can leap 50 times their own body length — what are they?
Flea: Insects of the order Siphonaptera. Flea, the common name for the order Siphonaptera, includes 2,500 species of small flightless insects that live as external parasites of mammals and birds.
Found in the rainforests and savannas of sub-Saharan Africa, this snake has the longest fangs of any venomous species — up to two inches — and the highest venom yield of any snake — which snake?
Gaboon viper: Species of snake. It is the largest member of the genus Bitis.
Known only from teeth and four jawbones, this extinct genus of giant ape roamed China for nearly two million years and is now thought to be a close relative of the orangutan — what is it?
Gigantopithecus: Extinct genus of primate. The species may have been sexually dimorphic, with males much bigger than females.

Native from Mexico down to southern Brazil, this large arboreal lizard can grow past six feet long, is a popular but demanding pet, and has become invasive in many warm regions worldwide — which species?
Green iguana: Species of reptile. Usually, this animal is simply called the iguana.

Named after a bird of prey, this British-developed attack aircraft was the only truly successful vertical-takeoff design of its era, able to fly from car parks and forest clearings instead of vulnerable airbases — which aircraft?
Harrier jump jet: Multirole combat aircraft family by Hawker Siddeley, later British Aerospace.

A Greek physician and philosopher of the classical era, this figure is hailed as the "Father of Medicine" for championing prognosis, clinical observation, and the now-discredited theory of bodily humors — who is he?
Hippocrates: Ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE)
Though phylogenetically closer to cats, these African carnivores resemble dogs thanks to convergent evolution, and their family has just four living species — what animal is it?
This probability principle holds that a randomly typing creature, given endless time, would almost surely reproduce the complete works of Shakespeare — what's it called?
Infinite monkey theorem: Counterintuitive result in probability.

A Manhattan Project veteran, this American physicist won a share of the 1975 Nobel Prize for proposing that not all atomic nuclei are spherical — an idea later confirmed by Aage Bohr and Ben Mottelson. Who was he?
James Rainwater: American physicist. Rainwater joined the physics faculty at Columbia in 1946, where he reached the rank of full professor in 1952 and was named Pupin Professor of Physics in 1982.
Dubbed the 'Angel of Death,' this German physician held doctorates in both anthropology and medicine before joining the SS and selecting Auschwitz prisoners for the gas chambers — who was he?
Josef Mengele: Nazi SS doctor at Auschwitz (1911–1979)
Made from shredded pastry dough layered with cheese and soaked in sugar syrup, this Arab dessert is especially popular during Ramadan, with a famous variant hailing from Nablus — what is it?

An Atlanta factory superintendent with a Cornell engineering degree, he was wrongly convicted of murdering a young employee, then kidnapped from prison and lynched — a case that became a focus of antisemitism. Who was he?
Nicknamed "Connie" and instantly recognizable by its triple tail and dolphin-shaped fuselage, which four-engined airliner was the first civil aircraft family to widely use a pressurized cabin?
Lockheed Constellation: Family of US airliners with 4 piston engines, 1943.
This age-related eye disease gradually damages the retina's central region, with a 'wet' form involving leaking blood vessels and a 'dry' form marked by deposits called drusen — what is it?
Macular degeneration: Vision loss due to damage to the macula of the eye.

Endemic to North America and known for long, upward-curving upper tusks with little to no lower tusks, this proboscidean's genus split from other elephant relatives at least 28 million years ago — which ancient beast?
In medicine, this term describes a disease spreading from a primary site to a secondary one — most often used for a cancer seeding new tumors elsewhere in the body — what is it?
Metastasis: Spreading of a disease inside a body. The newly pathological sites, then, are metastases (mets).
Cultivated by the Aztecs and named partly for a Mexican state capital, this flower opens each evening between four and eight o'clock and perfumes the night before closing by morning — which plant?

Mirabilis jalapa: Species of flower. Mirabilis jalapa, the marvel of Peru or four o'clock flower, is the most commonly grown ornamental species of Mirabilis plant, and is available in a range of colors.
Sold under the brand name Bactroban, this topical antibiotic treats impetigo and clears MRSA from the nose — what is it?
Derived from the Greek word for kidney, this medical specialty covers kidney function, disease, and treatments ranging from diet changes to dialysis and transplantation — which field?
Nephrology: Medical study concerned with the kidneys.
Built from nucleotide units — a sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base — this biomolecule class includes both DNA and RNA. Which class of molecule?
Nucleic acid: Class of large biomolecules essential to all known life.
Nicknamed the fish hawk, this diurnal bird of prey has a wingspan up to 180 centimeters and hunts almost exclusively fish — which bird?
Osprey: Species of bird. The osprey (Pandion haliaetus), historically known as sea hawk, river hawk, and fish hawk, is a diurnal, fish-eating bird of prey with a cosmopolitan range.

First described by a 17th-century French mathematician in 1653, this fluid mechanics principle states that a pressure change at any point in a confined, incompressible fluid is felt equally throughout it — what's it called?
Pascal's law: Principle in fluid mechanics. The law was established by French mathematician Blaise Pascal in 1653 and published in 1663.
Called the 'father of transplantation,' this Brazilian-born biologist won a 1960 Nobel for his work on acquired immune tolerance and graft rejection — who was he?

Cultivated for its edible nuts since prehistoric times and native to the Mediterranean and the Levant, this pine species has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit — which species?
Pinus pinea: Species of pine tree. Pinus pinea, the Italian stone pine or Mediterranean stone pine, is a tree from the pine family, Pinaceae.
Stockpiled for radiation emergencies, this oral compound floods and shields the thyroid gland — and also treats hyperthyroidism and the skin infection sporotrichosis. Which compound is it?

Harvested from Plantago seeds mainly grown in northern India, this dietary fiber relieves both constipation and mild diarrhea, and can modestly lower cholesterol and blood pressure with regular use. What is it?
Psyllium: Plant used as a dietary fiber.
This genus of muroid rodents gives its scientific name to the common rat, though not every animal called a rat actually belongs to it — which genus?
Sold under the brand name Rituxan, this monoclonal antibody treats non-Hodgkin lymphoma, rheumatoid arthritis and several other autoimmune conditions via slow IV infusion — what is it?
Named after a 19th-century American veterinary surgeon, this genus of rod-shaped, flagella-covered bacteria includes over 2,650 serotypes divided among just two species — what is it?
Salmonella: Genus of bacteria. Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped, (bacillus) Gram-negative bacteria of the family Enterobacteriaceae.
This class of central nervous system depressant increases GABA activity to calm irritability and anxiety, distinct from drugs used mainly to induce sleep — what is it?
Sedative: Drug that reduces excitement without inducing sleep.
In this rare congenital condition affecting about 1 in 10,000 people, the heart and other major organs sit as a mirror image of their normal position — what's it called?
Situs inversus: Condition in which organs are reversed.

Made of a segmented series of bones cushioned by intervertebral discs, this defining feature of some 50,000 animal species surrounds and protects the nerve tissue running through it — what is it, also known as the backbone?
Spinal column: Bony structure found in vertebrates.

This small nocturnal marsupial has membranes stretching from its forelegs to hindlegs that let it soar between trees, and its scientific name translates to 'short-headed rope-dancer' — what animal is it?
Sugar glider: Species of Australian marsupial.
A staple from the Caribbean to Oceania to East Asia, this Araceae-family plant is prized for the starchy underground corm it grows much like a yam — what is it?
Taro: Species of plant. Taro (Colocasia esculenta) is a root vegetable.
This English economist and cleric argued in an 1798 essay that population growth would always outpace food production gains, dooming society to hardship — who is he?
Thomas Robert Malthus: British political economist (1766–1834)
